title: Plant Biology: The Greenhouse Lab
subtitle: Cook food with sunlight, label a real seedling, and launch seeds into the world.

learningFocus.summary: In this lab the student runs a working greenhouse: feeding a growing plant the three ingredients of photosynthesis, labelling the real parts of a germinating seedling from an actual photograph, and launching seeds toward the dispersal method that matches how they really travel in nature. This builds scientific enquiry through noticing, questioning and testing, and strengthens analytical thinking as the student links a cause (sunlight, water, carbon dioxide) to an effect (glucose and oxygen) and connects a seed's shape to its method of travel. Creativity and problem-solving come from matching real photographed structures to their function under time pressure, and communication is practised in writing up why photosynthesis matters and how seed dispersal helps a plant survive. The content practised is Primary 2 Science, Biology, Module 1: Plants — photosynthesis, the jobs of roots/stem/leaves/flowers, and seed dispersal — the foundation every later biology topic about living things builds on.

orient.objective: Explain what a plant needs to make its own food, how its different parts work together, and how new plants get started from seeds.
orient.courseLink: Primary 2 Science, Biology, Module 1: Plants — the foundation for every later topic about living things.
successCriteria: I can say what a plant needs for photosynthesis, and what it makes.
I can match a real seedling's roots, stem and seed leaf to the job each one does.
I can explain how a seed's shape helps it travel away from its parent plant.
orient.mission: Step into the greenhouse. You are the plant's chef, its doctor, and its travel agent — all in one shift.
steps: Notice real details on a photo of a germinating seedling.
Say which question this investigation is really answering.
Write your hypothesis before you touch anything.
Work through all three greenhouse stations.
Your results log into your Investigation Record by themselves.
Explain, apply, answer the Knowledge Check, then reflect.
Press Generate Learning Evidence to download your work.
orient.realLife: Every salad on your plate, every park you walk through, and every dandelion seed that drifts past your window is a plant doing exactly what you are about to discover — cooking its own food from sunlight, and sending its seeds out to find a new home.
orient.scientificObservation: A bean seed grown in a dark cupboard for two weeks comes out tall, pale yellow and floppy. The same bean seed grown on a sunny windowsill comes out short, sturdy and deep green.
orient.scientificQuestion: What does a plant actually need to grow well, and how do its different parts help it survive?

observation.title: Meet a Real Seedling
observation.lede: Before you learn any names, look closely at a real photograph and notice what is actually there.

question.prompt: You just compared a bean seedling grown in the dark with one grown in sunlight. Which question is this investigation really designed to answer?
question.hint: Pick the one real, testable question — not just a fact about one seedling.

options.label: What does a plant need to grow well, and how do its parts help it survive?
What is the tallest plant ever recorded?
Do plants prefer the colour green?
How many leaves does one bean plant have?

predict.prompt: If a healthy plant is kept in a dark cupboard for two weeks, what do you predict will happen, and why?
predict.hint: Think about what leaves actually need in order to make food.

options.label: It will grow tall, pale and weak, because without light it cannot make chlorophyll or food.
It will grow shorter but greener, because darkness helps a plant save energy.
It will grow exactly the same as a plant in sunlight, because leaves don't need light.
It will die within a day, because darkness is poisonous to plants.

investigate.title: The Greenhouse Lab
investigate.lede: Work through all three stations below — cook food for the plant, label a real seedling, and launch seeds toward the way they really travel.

record.intro: Every station you complete logs itself here automatically — this is your evidence.
record.emptyText: No results yet. Go back to the Greenhouse Lab and try a station.

explain.prompt: Look at your Investigation Record from the Photosynthesis Kitchen. Explain what a plant needs to make its own food, and why it releases oxygen as well as making glucose.
explain.lede: Use your own completed Kitchen cycles from the Investigation Record as evidence.
explain.frame: Try this shape: "A plant needs ___, ___ and ___ to make food. The green chemical called ___ traps the sunlight energy. The plant makes ___ (its food) and releases ___ as a leftover gas."

markingScheme.criterion: Names all three photosynthesis ingredients used at the Kitchen station: sunlight (light), water and carbon dioxide, AND states that the plant makes glucose (food) from them.
markingScheme.accept: Any correct naming of the three ingredients and glucose/food/sugar as the product, in the student's own words, referring to their own completed Kitchen cycles.
markingScheme.insufficient: Naming only one or two ingredients, or never stating that food/glucose is made.

markingScheme.criterion: States that chlorophyll, the green substance in the leaves, is what traps or absorbs the sunlight's energy to power the reaction.
markingScheme.accept: Any correct statement linking chlorophyll (or 'the green stuff in leaves') to trapping/absorbing light energy.
markingScheme.insufficient: Saying leaves are 'green' with no mention of chlorophyll trapping light energy.

markingScheme.criterion: Explains that oxygen is released as a by-product / leftover gas of making food, not the main goal of the process — the plant's main job is making glucose, and oxygen is what comes out alongside it.
markingScheme.accept: Any scientifically valid phrasing of oxygen as a by-product released into the air; exact keywords not required.
markingScheme.insufficient: Stating 'plants make oxygen' with no sense that it is a by-product of making food, or confusing it with the main product.

apply.prompt: A courgette (zucchini) plant only grows fruit on flowers that bees have visited, and its seeds later get carried far away inside the droppings of animals that eat the fruit. Using what you discovered about flowers and seed dispersal, give TWO reasons why this actually helps the plant survive.
apply.lede: This is a real problem every flowering plant has to solve. Think about what a flower is for, and what happens if every seed lands right next to its parent.
apply.frame: Give two clear reasons. Think about pollination (Reason 1) and what happens if seeds don't travel away from the parent plant (Reason 2).

markingScheme.criterion: Reason 1 (pollination): states that bees carry pollen between flowers, and that without this pollination the plant cannot make seeds or fruit.
markingScheme.accept: Any correct statement that bees pollinate the flowers and that this is needed to produce seeds/fruit; exact wording not required.
markingScheme.insufficient: Saying 'bees visit flowers' with no mention of pollen or that pollination is needed to make seeds/fruit.

markingScheme.criterion: Reason 2 (dispersal): explains that seeds carried away inside an animal and dropped far from the parent plant land somewhere new, so the new seedlings are not competing with the parent (or each other) for light, water, space and nutrients.
markingScheme.accept: Any correct statement that dispersal moves seeds away from the parent to reduce competition for resources.
markingScheme.insufficient: Saying 'the seeds get carried away' with no mention of why moving away from the parent actually helps (reduced competition).

markingScheme.criterion: Both reasons name a genuine mechanism (pollination enabling seed/fruit production; dispersal reducing competition) rather than a vague statement like 'bees help' or 'seeds travel' with no explanation of why that matters to the plant's survival.
markingScheme.accept: Also accept a correctly reasoned mention that animal dispersal can also give a seed a ready-made patch of fertiliser (droppings), provided both required reasons above are still clearly present with their mechanisms.
markingScheme.insufficient: Two reasons stated but neither explains the underlying mechanism.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Match each part of the plant to the job it does.

pairs.right: Absorb water and nutrients from the soil, and anchor the plant
Holds the leaves up to the light and transports water and food
Use sunlight, water and carbon dioxide to make food
Makes seeds, often with the help of pollinators like bees

knowledgeCheck.explain: Roots anchor and absorb. The stem is the plant's highway, transporting water up and food down. Leaves are the kitchen, where photosynthesis happens. The flower is the reproductive part, making the seeds of the next generation.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: In the Photosynthesis Kitchen, which gas did the plant take in from the air to make its food?
knowledgeCheck.explain: Carbon dioxide enters through tiny openings on the leaf called stomata. Combined with water and sunlight energy, it is turned into glucose — and oxygen is released.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: A dandelion seed has a fluffy, feathery 'parachute'. Which method of seed dispersal is this shape an adaptation for?
knowledgeCheck.explain: A light, fluffy parachute shape catches the breeze and can carry a dandelion seed a long way from its parent plant — exactly what you tested at the Launch Pad.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Photosynthesis keeps refilling the air with the oxygen every animal needs to breathe. About what percentage of the air around us is oxygen?
knowledgeCheck.explain: Air is about 21% oxygen (and roughly 78% nitrogen). Plants and algae doing photosynthesis are what keep that oxygen level topped up.

rubric.note: You are graded out of 15 marks, shown as a percentage. The Knowledge Check is marked for you automatically; your teacher marks the two written answers.

criteria.label: Knowledge & understanding
criteria.descriptor: Plant parts, photosynthesis gases, dandelion dispersal, and oxygen in the air — all correct in the Knowledge Check.
criteria.source: Auto-marked from the Knowledge Check (auto_marked_score) — the teacher does not mark this row.

criteria.label: Use of evidence
criteria.source: = the Explain question's 3-point marking scheme above, one-to-one. Do not award these marks a second time here.

levels.descriptor: No photosynthesis ingredients or products correctly named.
Names some ingredients and the food product, but chlorophyll and the by-product gas are missing or wrong.
Names the ingredients, food product and chlorophyll's role, with a gap in explaining oxygen as a by-product.
Names sunlight, water and carbon dioxide, states the plant makes glucose, explains chlorophyll traps the light energy, and explains oxygen is released as a by-product.

criteria.label: Scientific reasoning
criteria.source: = the Apply question's 3-point marking scheme above, one-to-one. Do not award these marks a second time here.

levels.descriptor: No valid reason given, or reasons do not relate to pollination or dispersal.
Gives one correct reason (pollination or dispersal) but without a mechanism, e.g. just 'bees help' or 'seeds travel'.
Gives one full mechanism-based reason (pollination needed to make seeds, OR dispersal reduces competition) plus a second, weaker reason.
Gives two correct, mechanism-based reasons: bees pollinate flowers so seeds/fruit can form, AND dispersal moves seeds away so new plants avoid competing with the parent for resources.

criteria.label: Communication
criteria.source: Assessed holistically across BOTH the Explain and Apply answers together — independent of, and never overlapping with, the content marks in use_of_evidence and reasoning above.

levels.descriptor: Too unclear or incomplete for the reasoning to be followed reliably.
Main meaning is understandable, but organisation, precision or vocabulary has problems.
Clear and logical, uses appropriate subject vocabulary (e.g. chlorophyll, pollination, dispersal), precise enough to follow easily.

markingInstructions: Mark ONLY the two constructed responses (Explain, Apply). Award marks point-by-point using each question's marking_scheme in marking_context: each point is worth the marks stated, is independent unless it names a dependsOn point (in which case only award it if that earlier point was also awarded), and each point's 'accept'/'insufficient' tell you exactly what does and doesn't count. use_of_evidence's 3 marks ARE the Explain marking_scheme's 3 points, and reasoning's 3 marks ARE the Apply marking_scheme's 3 points — the rubric levels restate the same points as bands; award each set of 3 marks ONCE, not twice. communication is a separate, holistic 2 marks across both answers' clarity and vocabulary, never overlapping with the content marks. Copy auto_marked_score into knowledge_accuracy (7 marks = full). Use the student's own logged Investigation Record (the station/item/outcome columns in simulation_results.trials) to check that any claim they make about the Kitchen station is consistent with what they actually did. Accept scientifically valid alternative wording and do not penalise spelling unless meaning is unclear. Total is out of 15 (7 auto + 3 + 3 + 2); report the percentage, one strength, one correction, and one next step, in under 80 words.

es.title: Biología Vegetal: El Laboratorio del Invernadero
es.subtitle: Cocina alimento con luz solar, etiqueta una plántula real y lanza semillas al mundo.

learningFocus.summary: En este laboratorio el estudiante dirige un invernadero en funcionamiento: alimenta una planta con los tres ingredientes de la fotosíntesis, etiqueta las partes reales de una plántula germinando a partir de una fotografía auténtica, y lanza semillas hacia el método de dispersión que realmente coincide con su forma. Esto desarrolla la indagación científica mediante la observación, la pregunta y la prueba, y fortalece el pensamiento analítico al vincular una causa (luz solar, agua, dióxido de carbono) con un efecto (glucosa y oxígeno) y al conectar la forma de una semilla con su método de viaje. La creatividad y la resolución de problemas surgen al emparejar estructuras fotografiadas reales con su función, y la comunicación se practica al explicar por qué importa la fotosíntesis y cómo la dispersión de semillas ayuda a la planta a sobrevivir. El contenido practicado es Ciencias de Primaria 2, Biología, Módulo 1: Las Plantas — la fotosíntesis, las funciones de raíces, tallo, hojas y flores, y la dispersión de semillas — la base sobre la que se construye cada tema posterior de biología.

orient.objective: Explicar qué necesita una planta para fabricar su propio alimento, cómo trabajan juntas sus distintas partes, y cómo empiezan las plantas nuevas a partir de semillas.
orient.courseLink: Ciencias de Primaria 2, Biología, Módulo 1: Las Plantas — la base de todos los temas posteriores sobre los seres vivos.
successCriteria: Puedo decir qué necesita una planta para la fotosíntesis, y qué produce.
Puedo relacionar las raíces, el tallo y la hoja semilla de una plántula real con la función de cada una.
Puedo explicar cómo la forma de una semilla le ayuda a viajar lejos de su planta madre.
orient.mission: Entra al invernadero. Eres el chef de la planta, su médico y su agente de viajes — todo en un mismo turno.
steps: Observa detalles reales en una foto de una plántula germinando.
Di qué pregunta responde realmente esta investigación.
Escribe tu hipótesis antes de tocar nada.
Trabaja en las tres estaciones del invernadero.
Tus resultados se registran solos en tu Registro de Investigación.
Explica, aplica, responde la Comprobación y luego reflexiona.
Pulsa Generar Evidencia de Aprendizaje para descargar tu trabajo.
orient.realLife: Cada ensalada en tu plato, cada parque por el que caminas, y cada semilla de diente de león que flota junto a tu ventana es una planta haciendo exactamente lo que estás a punto de descubrir — cocinar su propio alimento con luz solar, y enviar sus semillas a buscar un nuevo hogar.

observation.title: Conoce una Plántula Real
observation.lede: Antes de aprender ningún nombre, observa de cerca una fotografía real y anota lo que realmente ves.

question.prompt: Acabas de comparar una plántula de judía crecida en la oscuridad con una crecida con luz solar. ¿Qué pregunta responde realmente esta investigación?
question.hint: Elige la única pregunta real y comprobable — no solo un dato sobre una plántula.

options.label: ¿Qué necesita una planta para crecer bien, y cómo ayudan sus partes a sobrevivir?
¿Cuál es la planta más alta jamás registrada?
¿Cuántas hojas tiene una planta de judía?

predict.prompt: Si una planta sana se guarda en un armario oscuro durante dos semanas, ¿qué predices que pasará, y por qué?
predict.hint: Piensa en lo que las hojas realmente necesitan para fabricar alimento.

options.label: Crecerá alta, pálida y débil, porque sin luz no puede fabricar clorofila ni alimento.
Crecerá más baja pero más verde, porque la oscuridad le ayuda a ahorrar energía.
Crecerá exactamente igual que con luz solar, porque las hojas no necesitan luz.
Morirá en un día, porque la oscuridad es venenosa para las plantas.

investigate.title: El Laboratorio del Invernadero
investigate.lede: Trabaja en las tres estaciones — cocina alimento para la planta, etiqueta una plántula real, y lanza semillas según su forma real de viajar. El agua está disponible en todas las estaciones a propósito.

record.intro: Cada estación que completas se registra aquí sola — esta es tu evidencia.
record.emptyText: Todavía no hay resultados. Vuelve al Laboratorio del Invernadero y prueba una estación.

explain.prompt: Mira tu Registro de Investigación de la Cocina de la Fotosíntesis. Explica qué necesita una planta para fabricar su propio alimento, y por qué libera oxígeno además de fabricar glucosa.
explain.lede: Usa tus propios ciclos completados en la Cocina como evidencia.

apply.prompt: Una planta de calabacín solo produce fruto en las flores que han visitado las abejas, y sus semillas después son transportadas lejos dentro de los excrementos de los animales que comen el fruto. Usando lo que descubriste sobre las flores y la dispersión de semillas, da DOS razones por las que esto ayuda a la planta a sobrevivir.
apply.lede: Piensa en la polinización (Razón 1) y en qué pasa si todas las semillas caen junto a su planta madre (Razón 2).

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Relaciona cada parte de la planta con la función que realiza.

pairs.right: Absorben agua y nutrientes del suelo, y anclan la planta
Sostiene las hojas hacia la luz y transporta agua y alimento
Usan luz solar, agua y dióxido de carbono para fabricar alimento
Fabrica semillas, a menudo con ayuda de polinizadores como las abejas

knowledgeCheck.explain: Las raíces anclan y absorben. El tallo es la autopista de la planta, transportando agua hacia arriba y alimento hacia abajo. Las hojas son la cocina, donde ocurre la fotosíntesis. La flor es la parte reproductiva, que fabrica las semillas de la siguiente generación.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: En la Cocina de la Fotosíntesis, ¿qué gas tomó la planta del aire para fabricar su alimento?
knowledgeCheck.explain: El dióxido de carbono entra por unas aberturas diminutas de la hoja llamadas estomas. Combinado con agua y la energía de la luz solar, se transforma en glucosa — y se libera oxígeno.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Una semilla de diente de león tiene un 'paracaídas' plumoso. ¿Para qué método de dispersión es una adaptación esta forma?
knowledgeCheck.explain: Una forma ligera y plumosa atrapa la brisa y puede llevar una semilla de diente de león muy lejos de su planta madre — justo lo que probaste en la Plataforma de Lanzamiento.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: La fotosíntesis mantiene el aire lleno del oxígeno que todo animal necesita para respirar. ¿Aproximadamente qué porcentaje del aire que nos rodea es oxígeno?
knowledgeCheck.explain: El aire es aproximadamente 21% oxígeno (y unos 78% nitrógeno). Las plantas y algas que hacen fotosíntesis son las que mantienen ese nivel de oxígeno.

rubric.note: Tu nota son los 15 puntos posibles, mostrados como porcentaje. La Comprobación de Conocimientos se corrige automáticamente; tu profesor corrige las dos respuestas escritas.

criteria.label: Conocimiento y comprensión
criteria.descriptor: Partes de la planta, gases de la fotosíntesis, dispersión del diente de león y oxígeno en el aire — todo correcto en la Comprobación.

levels.descriptor: No se nombra correctamente ningún ingrediente ni producto de la fotosíntesis.
Nombra algunos ingredientes y el producto alimenticio, pero falta la clorofila o el gas subproducto.
Nombra los ingredientes, el producto alimenticio y el papel de la clorofila, con un vacío al explicar el oxígeno como subproducto.
Nombra luz solar, agua y dióxido de carbono, dice que la planta fabrica glucosa, explica que la clorofila atrapa la energía de la luz, y explica que el oxígeno se libera como subproducto.
No se da ninguna razón válida, o las razones no se relacionan con la polinización ni la dispersión.
Da una razón correcta (polinización o dispersión) pero sin mecanismo, por ejemplo solo 'las abejas ayudan'.
Da una razón completa con mecanismo (la polinización es necesaria para formar semillas, O la dispersión reduce la competencia) más una segunda razón más débil.

Da dos razones correctas con mecanismo: las abejas polinizan las flores para que se formen semillas/frutos, Y la dispersión aleja las semillas para que las nuevas plantas no compitan con la madre por los recursos.
Demasiado confuso o incompleto para seguir el razonamiento con fiabilidad.
El significado principal se entiende, pero la organización, precisión o vocabulario tiene problemas.
Claro y lógico, usa vocabulario apropiado (por ejemplo clorofila, polinización, dispersión), lo bastante preciso para seguirlo con facilidad.
